title: Episode 1 — Telemachus
paragraphs: Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came up from the stairhead, carrying a bowl of shaving lather with a mirror and razor laid crosswise on top. A yellow dressing gown, untied, floated gently behind him in the mild morning air. He held the bowl up high and chanted:
—Introibo ad altare Dei — I will go unto the altar of God.
He stopped, peered down the dark winding stairs, and called out roughly:
—Come up, Kinch! Come up, you cowardly Jesuit!

With mock solemnity he stepped forward and mounted the round gun platform. He turned and gravely blessed the tower three times, then the surrounding countryside and the waking mountains. Then, catching sight of Stephen Dedalus, he leaned toward him and made rapid signs of the cross in the air, gurgling in his throat and shaking his head. Stephen Dedalus, annoyed and sleepy, leaned his arms on top of the staircase and looked coldly at the shaking, gurgling face blessing him — long as a horse's — and at the light unshorn hair, textured and colored like pale oak.
Buck Mulligan peeked for an instant under the mirror and then smartly covered the bowl.
—Back to barracks! he said sternly.
He added in a preacher's tone:

—For this, O dearly beloved, is the genuine Christ: body and soul and blood and wounds. Slow music, please. Shut your eyes, gentlemen. One moment. A little trouble with those white blood cells. Silence, all.

He peered sideways upward and gave a long slow whistle, then paused in rapt attention, his even white teeth gleaming here and there with gold fillings. Golden-mouthed. Two strong shrill whistles answered through the calm.
—Thanks, old chap, he cried briskly. That'll do nicely. Switch off the current, will you?

He hopped off the gun platform and looked gravely at his watcher, gathering the loose folds of his gown around his legs. The plump shadowed face and heavy oval jaw recalled a medieval bishop, a patron of the arts. A pleasant smile spread quietly across his lips.
—The mockery of it! he said cheerfully. Your absurd name, an ancient Greek!

He pointed his finger in friendly jest and went over to the parapet, laughing to himself. Stephen Dedalus got up, followed him wearily halfway, and sat down on the edge of the gun platform, watching as Mulligan propped his mirror on the parapet, dipped the brush in the bowl, and lathered his cheeks and neck.
Buck Mulligan's cheerful voice went on.

—My name is absurd too: Malachi Mulligan, two dactyls. But it has a Greek ring, hasn't it? Light and sunny like the buck himself. We must go to Athens. Will you come if I can get the aunt to cough up twenty pounds?
He laid the brush aside and, laughing with delight, cried:
—Will he come? The starving Jesuit!
He stopped laughing and began to shave with care.
—Tell me, Mulligan, Stephen said quietly.
—Yes, my love?
—How long is Haines going to stay in this tower?
Buck Mulligan showed a shaven cheek over his right shoulder.

—God, isn't he dreadful? he said frankly. A ponderous Englishman. He thinks you're not a gentleman. God, these bloody English! Bursting with money and indigestion. Because he comes from Oxford. You know, Dedalus, you have the real Oxford manner. He can't figure you out. Oh, my name for you is the best: Kinch, the knife-blade.
He shaved carefully over his chin.
—He was raving all night about a black panther, Stephen said. Where is his gun case?
—A total lunatic! Mulligan said. Were you frightened?

—I was, Stephen said with energy and growing fear. Out here in the dark with a man I don't know raving and moaning to himself about shooting a black panther. You've saved men from drowning. I'm not a hero, though. If he stays on here, I'm leaving.
Buck Mulligan frowned at the lather on his razor blade. He hopped down from his perch and began searching his trouser pockets hastily.
—Damn! he cried thickly.
He came over to the gun platform and, thrusting a hand into Stephen's upper pocket, said:
—Lend us your handkerchief to wipe my razor.
Stephen let him pull out and hold up by its corner a dirty crumpled handkerchief. Buck Mulligan wiped the razor blade neatly. Then, gazing over the handkerchief, he said:
—The poet's hanky! A new art color for our Irish poets: snot-green. You can almost taste it, can't you?
He climbed back up to the parapet and gazed out over Dublin Bay, his fair oak-pale hair stirring slightly.

—God! he said quietly. Isn't the sea what Swinburne calls it: a great sweet mother? The snot-green sea. The ball-tightening sea. Epi oinopa ponton — upon the wine-dark sea. Ah, Dedalus, the Greeks! I must teach you. You must read them in the original. Thalatta! Thalatta! — The sea! The sea! She is our great sweet mother. Come and look.
Stephen stood up and went over to the parapet. Leaning on it, he looked down at the water and at the mail boat clearing the harbor mouth of Kingstown.
—Our mighty mother! Buck Mulligan said.
He turned abruptly, his grey searching eyes moving from the sea to Stephen's face.
—The aunt thinks you killed your mother, he said. That's why she won't let me have anything to do with you.
—Someone killed her, Stephen said gloomily.

—You could have knelt down, damn it, Kinch, when your dying mother asked you, Buck Mulligan said. I'm as much of a freethinker as you. But to think of your mother begging you with her last breath to kneel down and pray for her. And you refused. There is something sinister in you....
He broke off and lightly lathered his farther cheek again. A tolerant smile curled his lips.
—But a lovely performer! he murmured to himself. Kinch, the loveliest performer of them all!
He shaved evenly and with care, in silence, seriously.

Stephen, an elbow resting on the jagged granite, leaned his palm against his brow and gazed at the fraying edge of his shiny black coat sleeve. Pain, not yet the pain of love, gnawed at his heart. Silently, in a dream, she had come to him after her death, her wasted body in its loose brown grave clothes giving off a smell of wax and rosewood, her breath bending over him, mute, reproachful, a faint smell of dampened ashes. Across the threadbare cuff he saw the sea hailed as a great sweet mother by the well-fed voice beside him. The ring of bay and skyline held a dull green mass of liquid. A bowl of white china had stood beside her deathbed holding the green sluggish bile which she had torn up from her rotting liver in fits of loud groaning vomiting.
Buck Mulligan wiped his razor blade again.
—Ah, poor old Stephen! he said in a kind voice. I must give you a shirt and a few handkerchiefs. How are the secondhand trousers?
—They fit well enough, Stephen answered.
Buck Mulligan worked at the hollow beneath his lower lip.

—The mockery of it, he said contentedly. Secondhand legs they should be. God knows what diseased rogue wore them last. I have a lovely pair with a hair stripe, grey. You'll look splendid in them. I'm not joking, Kinch. You look damn good when you're dressed up.
—Thanks, Stephen said. I can't wear them if they're grey.
—He can't wear them, Buck Mulligan told his face in the mirror. Etiquette is etiquette. He kills his mother but he can't wear grey trousers.
He folded his razor neatly and with stroking fingertips felt the smooth skin.
Stephen turned his gaze from the sea to the plump face with its smoke-blue, lively eyes.

—That fellow I was with at the Ship pub last night, said Buck Mulligan, says you have general paralysis of the insane. He's up in the mental hospital with Connolly Norman. General paralysis of the insane!

He swept the mirror in a half circle through the air to flash the news abroad in the sunlight now radiant on the sea. His curling shaven lips laughed and the edges of his white glittering teeth. Laughter seized his whole strong, well-built body.
—Look at yourself, he said, you dreadful poet!

Stephen bent forward and peered at the mirror held out to him, cracked by a crooked line. Hair on end. As he and others see me. Who chose this face for me? This dog's body riddled with vermin. It asks me too.
—I pinched it from the maid's room, Buck Mulligan said. It does her fine. The aunt always keeps plain-looking servants for Malachi. Lead him not into temptation. And her name is Ursula.
Laughing again, he pulled the mirror away from Stephen's peering eyes.
—The rage of Caliban at not seeing his face in a mirror, he said. If Oscar Wilde were only alive to see you!
Drawing back and pointing, Stephen said with bitterness:
—It is a symbol of Irish art. The cracked looking glass of a servant.
Buck Mulligan suddenly linked his arm in Stephen's and walked with him round the tower, his razor and mirror clinking in the pocket where he had thrust them.
—It's not fair to tease you like that, Kinch, is it? he said kindly. God knows you have more spirit than any of them.
Parried again. He fears the blade of my art as I fear his. The cold steel pen.

—Cracked looking glass of a servant! Tell that to the English fellow downstairs and hit him up for a guinea. He's stinking with money and thinks you're not a gentleman. His old man made his fortune selling laxatives to Africans or some bloody swindle or other. God, Kinch, if you and I could only work together we might do something for this country. Hellenize it.
Cranly's arm. His arm.

—And to think of you having to beg from these swine. I'm the only one who knows what you are. Why don't you trust me more? What have you got against me? Is it Haines? If he makes any trouble here I'll bring down Seymour and we'll give him a beating worse than they gave Clive Kempthorpe.

Young shouts of wealthy voices in Clive Kempthorpe's rooms. Pale faces: they clutch their ribs with laughter, one grabbing another. Oh, I shall die! Break the news to her gently, Aubrey! I shall die! With the shredded ribbons of his shirt whipping the air he hops and hobbles around the table, trousers down at his heels, chased by Ades of Magdalen College with the tailor's shears. A terrified calf's face smeared with marmalade. I don't want to be debagged! Don't mess with me!

Shouts from the open window startling the evening in the quadrangle. A deaf gardener, aproned, with a face like the poet Matthew Arnold's, pushes his mower on the somber lawn, watching narrowly the dancing motes of grass blades.
To ourselves... new paganism... navel of the world.
—Let him stay, Stephen said. There's nothing wrong with him except at night.
—Then what is it? Buck Mulligan asked impatiently. Spit it out. I'm completely frank with you. What have you got against me now?
They stopped, looking toward the blunt cape of Bray Head lying on the water like the snout of a sleeping whale. Stephen freed his arm quietly.
—Do you want me to tell you? he asked.
—Yes, what is it? Buck Mulligan answered. I don't remember anything.
He looked into Stephen's face as he spoke. A light wind crossed his brow, softly fanning his fair uncombed hair and stirring silver points of anxiety in his eyes.
Stephen, depressed by his own voice, said:
—Do you remember the first day I went to your house after my mother's death?
Buck Mulligan frowned quickly and said:
—What? Where? I can't remember anything. I only remember ideas and sensations. Why? What happened in the name of God?
—You were making tea, Stephen said, and went across the landing to get more hot water. Your mother and some visitor came out of the drawing room. She asked you who was in your room.
—Yes? Buck Mulligan said. What did I say? I forget.
—You said, Stephen answered, Oh, it's only Dedalus whose mother is beastly dead.
A flush which made him look younger and more appealing rose to Buck Mulligan's cheek.
—Did I say that? he asked. Well? What harm is that?
He shook off his discomfort nervously.

—And what is death, he asked, your mother's or yours or my own? You only saw your mother die. I see them drop dead every day at the Mater Hospital and Richmond and cut up into pieces in the dissecting room. It's a beastly thing and nothing else. It simply doesn't matter. You wouldn't kneel down to pray for your mother on her deathbed when she asked you. Why? Because you have the cursed Jesuit streak in you, only it's been twisted the wrong way. To me it's all a mockery and beastly. Her brain was failing. She called the doctor Sir Peter Teazle and picked imaginary buttercups off the quilt. Humor her until it's over. You crossed her last wish in death and yet you sulk with me because I don't cry like some hired mourner from the undertaker's. Absurd! I suppose I did say it. I didn't mean to offend the memory of your mother.
He had talked himself into boldness. Stephen, shielding the gaping wounds the words had left in his heart, said very coldly:
—I am not thinking of the offense to my mother.
—Of what then? Buck Mulligan asked.
—Of the offense to me, Stephen answered.
Buck Mulligan swung round on his heel.
—Oh, an impossible person! he exclaimed.

He walked off quickly round the parapet. Stephen stood at his post, gazing over the calm sea toward the headland. Sea and headland now grew dim. Pulses were beating in his eyes, veiling their sight, and he felt the fever of his cheeks.
A voice within the tower called loudly:
—Are you up there, Mulligan?
—I'm coming, Buck Mulligan answered.
He turned toward Stephen and said:
—Look at the sea. What does it care about offenses? Forget your Jesuit brooding, Kinch, and come on down. The Englishman wants his morning bacon.
His head paused again for a moment at the top of the staircase, level with the roof:
—Don't brood over it all day, he said. I'm thoughtless. Give up the moody brooding.
His head vanished but the drone of his descending voice boomed out of the stairhead:

And no more turn aside and brood
Upon love's bitter mystery
For Fergus rules the brazen cars.

Shadows of trees floated silently through the morning peace from the stairhead seaward where he gazed. Inshore and farther out the mirror of water whitened, stirred by light-footed hurrying feet. White breast of the dim sea. The twining stresses, two by two. A hand plucking harp strings, merging their twining chords. Wave-white wedded words shimmering on the dim tide.

A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, wholly, shadowing the bay in deeper green. It lay beneath him, a bowl of bitter waters. Fergus's song: I sang it alone in the house, holding down the long dark chords. Her door was open: she wanted to hear my music. Silent with awe and pity I went to her bedside. She was crying in her wretched bed. For those words, Stephen: love's bitter mystery.
Where now?

Her secrets: old feathered fans, tasseled dance cards, powdered with musk, a string of amber beads in her locked drawer. A birdcage hung in the sunny window of her house when she was a girl. She heard old Royce sing in the pantomime of Turko the Terrible and laughed with others when he sang:

I am the boy
That can enjoy
Invisibility.
Ghost-like mirth, folded away: musk-perfumed.
And no more turn aside and brood.

Folded away in the memory of nature with her keepsakes. Memories besieged his brooding brain. Her glass of water from the kitchen tap when she had taken communion. A cored apple, filled with brown sugar, roasting for her at the fireside on a dark autumn evening. Her shapely fingernails reddened by the blood of lice crushed from the children's shirts.

In a dream, silently, she had come to him, her wasted body within its loose grave clothes giving off a smell of wax and rosewood, her breath bending over him with mute secret words, a faint smell of dampened ashes.

Her glazing eyes, staring out of death, to shake and bend my soul. On me alone. The death candle to light her agony. Ghostly light on the tortured face. Her hoarse loud breath rattling in horror, while all prayed on their knees. Her eyes on me to strike me down. Let the shining throng of confessors surround you: let the choir of rejoicing virgins receive you.
Ghoul! Chewer of corpses!
No, mother! Let me be and let me live.
—Kinch ahoy!

Buck Mulligan's voice sang from within the tower. It came nearer up the staircase, calling again. Stephen, still trembling at his soul's cry, heard warm running sunlight and in the air behind him friendly words.
—Dedalus, come down, like a good fellow. Breakfast is ready. Haines is apologizing for waking us last night. It's all right.
—I'm coming, Stephen said, turning.
—Do, for Jesus' sake, Buck Mulligan said. For my sake and for all our sakes.
His head disappeared and reappeared.
—I told him your line about Irish art. He says it's very clever. Hit him up for a pound, will you? A guinea, I mean.
—I get paid this morning, Stephen said.
—The school job? Buck Mulligan said. How much? Four pounds? Lend us one.
—If you want it, Stephen said.
—Four shining gold coins, Buck Mulligan cried with delight. We'll have a glorious drinking session to astonish the druidy druids. Four almighty sovereigns.
He flung up his hands and tramped down the stone stairs, singing out of tune with a Cockney accent:

Oh, won't we have a merry time,
Drinking whisky, beer and wine!
On coronation,
Coronation day!
Oh, won't we have a merry time
On coronation day!
Warm sunshine playing over the sea. The nickel shaving bowl gleamed, forgotten, on the parapet. Why should I bring it down? Or leave it there all day, forgotten friendship?

He went over to it, held it in his hands for a while, feeling its coolness, smelling the clammy residue of the lather in which the brush was stuck. Just as I carried the incense boat at Clongowes school. I am another person now and yet the same. A servant too. A server of a servant.

In the gloomy domed living room of the tower, Buck Mulligan's gowned form moved briskly back and forth around the hearth, hiding and revealing its yellow glow. Two shafts of soft daylight fell across the flagstone floor from the high narrow windows, and where their rays met, a cloud of coal smoke and frying fumes floated and turned.
—We'll be choked, Buck Mulligan said. Haines, open that door, will you?
Stephen laid the shaving bowl on the locker. A tall figure rose from the hammock where it had been sitting, went to the doorway and pulled open the inner doors.
—Have you the key? a voice asked.
—Dedalus has it, Buck Mulligan said. Good God, I'm choked!
He howled, without looking up from the fire:
—Kinch!
—It's in the lock, Stephen said, coming forward.

The key scraped round harshly twice and, when the heavy door had been pushed ajar, welcome light and bright air entered. Haines stood at the doorway, looking out. Stephen dragged his upended suitcase to the table and sat down to wait. Buck Mulligan tossed the fry onto the dish beside him. Then he carried the dish and a large teapot over to the table, set them down heavily, and sighed with relief.

—I'm melting, he said, as the candle remarked when... But hush! Not a word more on that subject! Kinch, wake up! Bread, butter, honey. Haines, come in. The food is ready. Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts. Where's the sugar? Oh damn, there's no milk.
Stephen fetched the loaf, the pot of honey, and the butter dish from the locker. Buck Mulligan sat down in a sudden huff.
—What sort of a dump is this? he said. I told her to come after eight.
—We can drink it black, Stephen said thirstily. There's a lemon in the locker.
—Oh, damn you and your Paris fads! Buck Mulligan said. I want Sandycove milk.
Haines came in from the doorway and said quietly:
—That woman is coming up with the milk.
—The blessings of God on you! Buck Mulligan cried, jumping up from his chair. Sit down. Pour out the tea there. The sugar is in the bag. Here, I can't go fumbling with the damn eggs.
He hacked through the fry on the dish and slapped it out on three plates, saying:
—In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
Haines sat down to pour out the tea.
—I'm giving you two lumps each, he said. But, I say, Mulligan, you do make strong tea, don't you?
Buck Mulligan, cutting thick slices from the loaf, said in an old woman's wheedling voice:
—When I makes tea I makes tea, as old mother Grogan said. And when I makes water I makes water.
—By Jove, it is tea, Haines said.
Buck Mulligan went on cutting and wheedling:
—So I do, Mrs Cahill, says she. Well, ma'am, says Mrs Cahill, God help you if you don't make them in the same pot.
He thrust a thick slice of bread, speared on his knife, toward each of his companions in turn.

—That's folklore, he said very earnestly, for your book, Haines. Five lines of text and ten pages of notes about the folk legends and fish-gods of Dundrum. Printed by the weird sisters in the year of the big wind.
He turned to Stephen and asked in a mock-puzzled voice, raising his brows:
—Can you recall, brother, is mother Grogan's tea and water pot mentioned in the Mabinogion or is it in the Upanishads?
—I doubt it, said Stephen gravely.
—Do you now? Buck Mulligan said in the same tone. Your reasons, pray?
—I suspect, Stephen said as he ate, it didn't exist in or out of the Mabinogion. Mother Grogan was, one imagines, a relative of Mary Ann.
Buck Mulligan's face smiled with delight.
—Charming! he said in a precious sweet voice, showing his white teeth and blinking his eyes pleasantly. Do you think she was? Quite charming!
Then, suddenly darkening all his features, he growled in a hoarse rasping voice as he cut again vigorously at the loaf:
—For old Mary Ann
She doesn't care a damn.
But, hiking up her petticoats...
He crammed his mouth with fry and munched and droned.
The doorway was darkened by an entering form.
—The milk, sir!
—Come in, ma'am, Mulligan said. Kinch, get the jug.
An old woman came forward and stood by Stephen's elbow.
—That's a lovely morning, sir, she said. Glory be to God.
—To whom? Mulligan said, glancing at her. Ah, to be sure!
Stephen reached back and took the milk jug from the locker.
—The country people, Mulligan said to Haines casually, speak frequently of the collector of foreskins — meaning Christ.
—How much, sir? asked the old woman.
—A quart, Stephen said.

He watched her pour into the measure and then into the jug rich white milk, not hers. Old shrunken breasts. She poured again a measureful and a little extra. Old and secret she had entered from a morning world, maybe a messenger. She praised the goodness of the milk, pouring it out. Crouching by a patient cow at daybreak in the lush field, a witch on her toadstool, her wrinkled fingers quick at the squirting teats. They lowed around her whom they knew, silky-coated cattle. Silk of the kine and poor old woman — names given her in old times, names for Ireland herself. A wandering old woman, humble form of an immortal, serving her conqueror and her cheerful betrayer, their common cuckold-queen, a messenger from the secret morning. To serve or to rebuke, whether he could not tell: but he scorned to beg her favor.
—It is indeed, ma'am, Buck Mulligan said, pouring milk into their cups.
—Taste it, sir, she said.
He drank at her bidding.

—If we could live on good food like that, he said to her somewhat loudly, we wouldn't have the country full of rotten teeth and rotten guts. Living in a bog, eating cheap food and the streets paved with dust, horse dung, and tuberculosis spit.
—Are you a medical student, sir? the old woman asked.
—I am, ma'am, Buck Mulligan answered.
—Look at that now, she said.

Stephen listened in scornful silence. She bows her old head to a voice that speaks to her loudly, her bone-setter, her medicine man: me she ignores. To the voice that will anoint and pray over her grave — all there is of her but her woman's unclean body, flesh not made in God's likeness, the serpent's prey. And to the loud voice that now commands her silence with wondering unsteady eyes.
—Do you understand what he says? Stephen asked her.
—Is it French you are talking, sir? the old woman said to Haines.
Haines spoke to her again at greater length, confidently.
—Irish, Buck Mulligan said. Do you speak Gaelic?
—I thought it was Irish, she said, by the sound of it. Are you from the west, sir?
—I am an Englishman, Haines answered.
—He's English, Buck Mulligan said, and he thinks we ought to speak Irish in Ireland.
—Sure we ought to, the old woman said, and I'm ashamed I don't speak the language myself. I'm told it's a grand language by them that knows.
—Grand is no name for it, said Buck Mulligan. Wonderful entirely. Fill us out some more tea, Kinch. Would you like a cup, ma'am?
—No, thank you, sir, the old woman said, slipping the ring of the milk can on her forearm and about to go.
Haines said to her:
—Have you your bill? We had better pay her, Mulligan, hadn't we?
Stephen filled the three cups again.

—Bill, sir? she said, halting. Well, it's seven mornings a pint at twopence is seven twos is a shilling and twopence over, and these three mornings a quart at fourpence is three quarts is a shilling. That's a shilling and one and two is two and two, sir.
Buck Mulligan sighed and, having filled his mouth with a crust thickly buttered on both sides, stretched out his legs and began to search his trouser pockets.
—Pay up and look pleasant, Haines said to him, smiling.
Stephen filled a third cup, a spoonful of tea faintly coloring the thick rich milk. Buck Mulligan produced a two-shilling coin, twisted it round in his fingers, and cried:
—A miracle!
He passed it along the table toward the old woman, saying:
—Ask nothing more of me, sweet. All I can give you I give.
Stephen laid the coin in her ungreedy hand.
—We'll owe twopence, he said.
—Time enough, sir, she said, taking the coin. Time enough. Good morning, sir.
She curtseyed and went out, followed by Buck Mulligan's tender chant:
—Heart of my heart, were it more,
More would be laid at your feet.
He turned to Stephen and said:
—Seriously, Dedalus. I'm broke. Hurry out to your school job and bring us back some money. Today the poets must drink and feast. Ireland expects that every man this day will do his duty.
—That reminds me, Haines said, rising, that I have to visit your national library today.
—Our swim first, Buck Mulligan said.
He turned to Stephen and asked blandly:
—Is this the day for your monthly wash, Kinch?
Then he said to Haines:
—The unwashed poet makes a point of bathing once a month.
—All Ireland is washed by the Gulf Stream, Stephen said as he let honey trickle over a slice of bread.
Haines, from the corner where he was knotting a scarf around the loose collar of his tennis shirt, spoke:
—I intend to make a collection of your sayings, if you will let me.
Speaking to me. They wash and scrub and clean. Remorse of conscience. Yet here's a spot that won't come out.
—That one about the cracked looking glass of a servant being the symbol of Irish art is awfully good.
Buck Mulligan kicked Stephen's foot under the table and said warmly:
—Wait till you hear him on Hamlet, Haines.
—Well, I mean it, Haines said, still speaking to Stephen. I was just thinking of it when that poor old woman came in.
—Would I make any money by it? Stephen asked.
Haines laughed and, as he took his soft grey hat from the hook on the hammock, said:
—I don't know, I'm sure.
He strolled out to the doorway. Buck Mulligan leaned across to Stephen and said with rough energy:
—You put your foot in it now. What did you say that for?
—Well? Stephen said. The problem is to get money. From whom? From the milk woman or from him. It's a toss-up, I think.
—I talk you up to him, Buck Mulligan said, and then you come along with your sneering look and your gloomy Jesuit jibes.
—I see little hope, Stephen said, from her or from him.
Buck Mulligan sighed tragically and laid his hand on Stephen's arm.
—From me, Kinch, he said.
In a suddenly changed tone he added:
—To tell you the God's truth I think you're right. Damn all else they're good for. Why don't you play them the way I do? To hell with them all. Let us get out of this dump.
He stood up, gravely untied and removed his gown, saying resignedly:
—Mulligan is stripped of his garments.
He emptied his pockets onto the table.
—There's your handkerchief, he said.

And putting on his stiff collar and rebellious tie he spoke to them, scolding them and his dangling watch chain. His hands plunged and rummaged in his trunk while he called for a clean handkerchief. God, we'll simply have to dress the part. I want purple gloves and green boots. Contradiction. Do I contradict myself? Very well then, I contradict myself. Mercurial Malachi. A limp black object flew out of his chattering hands.
—And there's your Latin Quarter hat, he said.
Stephen picked it up and put it on. Haines called to them from the doorway:
—Are you coming, you fellows?
—I'm ready, Buck Mulligan answered, going toward the door. Come out, Kinch. You've eaten all we left, I suppose. Resigned, he passed out with grave words and bearing, saying almost with sorrow:
—And going forth he met Butterly.
Stephen, taking his walking stick from its leaning place, followed them out and, as they went down the ladder, pulled the slow iron door shut and locked it. He put the huge key in his inner pocket.
At the foot of the ladder Buck Mulligan asked:
—Did you bring the key?
—I have it, Stephen said, going ahead of them.
He walked on. Behind him he heard Buck Mulligan swatting the young shoots of ferns or grasses with his heavy bath towel.
—Down, sir! How dare you, sir!
Haines asked:
—Do you pay rent for this tower?
—Twelve pounds, Buck Mulligan said.
—To the secretary of state for war, Stephen added over his shoulder.
They stopped while Haines surveyed the tower and said at last:
—Rather bleak in wintertime, I should say. Martello tower you call it?
—William Pitt had them built, Buck Mulligan said, when the French were threatening to invade. But ours is the omphalos — the navel of the world.
—What is your idea of Hamlet? Haines asked Stephen.
—No, no, Buck Mulligan shouted in mock pain. I'm not up to arguing with Thomas Aquinas and the fifty-five reasons he's marshaled to support it. Wait till I've had a few pints first.
He turned to Stephen, saying as he pulled down the lapels of his primrose waistcoat:
—You couldn't manage it without at least three pints, Kinch, could you?
—It has waited so long, Stephen said listlessly, it can wait longer.
—You pique my curiosity, Haines said amiably. Is it some paradox?

—Bah! Buck Mulligan said. We've outgrown Wilde and paradoxes. It's quite simple. He proves by algebra that Hamlet's grandson is Shakespeare's grandfather and that he himself is the ghost of his own father.
—What? Haines said, beginning to point at Stephen. He himself?
Buck Mulligan slung his towel like a stole around his neck and, bending in loose laughter, said to Stephen's ear:
—Oh, shade of Kinch the elder! Japhet in search of a father!
—We're always tired in the morning, Stephen said to Haines. And it is rather long to tell.
Buck Mulligan, walking forward again, raised his hands.
—Only a sacred pint can unbind the tongue of Dedalus, he said.
—I mean to say, Haines explained to Stephen as they followed, this tower and these cliffs here remind me somehow of Elsinore. That beetling cliff above the sea, isn't it?
Buck Mulligan turned suddenly for an instant toward Stephen but did not speak. In the bright silent instant Stephen saw his own image in cheap dusty mourning between their cheerful attire.
—It's a wonderful tale, Haines said, bringing them to a halt again.

Eyes pale as the sea the wind had freshened, paler, firm and prudent. The seas' ruler. He gazed southward over the bay, empty save for the smoke plume of the mail boat faint on the bright skyline and a sail tacking by the Muglins rocks.
—I read a theological interpretation of it somewhere, he said thoughtfully. The Father and the Son idea. The Son striving to be reconciled with the Father.

Buck Mulligan instantly put on a cheerful, broadly smiling face. He looked at them, his well-shaped mouth open happily, his eyes suddenly emptied of all shrewdness, blinking with mad gaiety. He moved his head like a puppet, the brims of his Panama hat quivering, and began to chant in a quiet happy foolish voice:

—I'm the queerest young fellow that ever you heard.
My mother's a Jew, my father's a bird.
With Joseph the joiner I cannot agree.
So here's to disciples and Calvary.
He held up a warning forefinger.

—If anyone thinks that I'm not divine
He'll get no free drinks when I'm making the wine
But have to drink water and wish it were plain
That I make when the wine becomes water again.

He tugged swiftly at Stephen's walking stick in farewell and, running forward to the brow of the cliff, fluttered his hands at his sides like fins or wings of one about to rise in the air, and chanted:

—Goodbye, now, goodbye! Write down all I said
And tell Tom, Dick and Harry I rose from the dead.
What's bred in the bone cannot fail me to fly
And Olivet's breezy... Goodbye, now, goodbye!

He capered ahead of them down toward the Forty Foot bathing spot, fluttering his winglike hands, leaping nimbly, his hat quivering in the fresh wind that carried back to them his brief birdlike cries.
Haines, who had been laughing guardedly, walked on beside Stephen and said:

—We oughtn't to laugh, I suppose. He's rather blasphemous. I'm not a believer myself, that is to say. Still, his good humor takes the harm out of it somehow, doesn't it? What did he call it? Joseph the Joiner?
—The ballad of joking Jesus, Stephen answered.
—Oh, Haines said, you have heard it before?
—Three times a day, after meals, Stephen said drily.
—You're not a believer, are you? Haines asked. I mean, a believer in the narrow sense of the word. Creation from nothing and miracles and a personal God.
—There's only one sense of the word, it seems to me, Stephen said.
Haines stopped to take out a smooth silver cigarette case in which a green stone twinkled. He sprang it open with his thumb and offered it.
—Thank you, Stephen said, taking a cigarette.

Haines helped himself and snapped the case shut. He put it back in his side pocket and took from his waistcoat pocket a nickel lighter, sprang it open too, and, having lit his cigarette, held the flame toward Stephen in the shell of his hands.
—Yes, of course, he said, as they walked on again. Either you believe or you don't, isn't it? Personally I couldn't stomach the idea of a personal God. You don't stand for that, I suppose?
—You behold in me, Stephen said with grim displeasure, a horrible example of free thought.

He walked on, waiting to be spoken to, trailing his walking stick by his side. Its metal tip followed lightly on the path, squealing at his heels. My familiar spirit, following me, calling, Steeeeeeeeeeeephen! A wavering line along the path. They will walk on it tonight, coming here in the dark. He wants that key. It is mine. I paid the rent. Now I eat his salt bread. Give him the key too. Everything. He will ask for it. That was in his eyes.
—After all, Haines began...
Stephen turned and saw that the cold gaze which had measured him was not entirely unkind.
—After all, I should think you are able to free yourself. You are your own master, it seems to me.
—I am a servant of two masters, Stephen said, an English and an Italian.
—Italian? Haines said.
A crazy queen, old and jealous. Kneel down before me.
—And a third, Stephen said, there is who wants me for odd jobs.
—Italian? Haines said again. What do you mean?
—The imperial British state, Stephen answered, his color rising, and the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic church.
Haines detached some fibers of tobacco from his lower lip before he spoke.
—I can quite understand that, he said calmly. An Irishman must think like that, I daresay. We feel in England that we have treated you rather unfairly. It seems history is to blame.

The proud powerful titles clanged through Stephen's memory, the triumph of their brazen bells: and one holy Catholic and apostolic church: the slow growth and change of rite and dogma like his own rare thoughts, a chemistry of stars. The voices blended in the Mass for Pope Marcellus, singing alone in loud affirmation: and behind their chant the vigilant angel of the church militant disarmed and menaced her heretics. A horde of heresies fleeing with crooked hats: Photius and the brood of mockers of whom Mulligan was one, and Arius, who fought his whole life long over whether the Son was of the same substance as the Father, and Valentine, who rejected Christ's earthly body, and the subtle African heretic Sabellius who held that the Father was Himself His own Son. Words Mulligan had spoken a moment ago in mockery to the stranger. Idle mockery. The void surely awaits all those who weave the wind: a menace, a disarming and a defeat from those embattled angels of the church, Michael's host, who defend her ever in the hour of conflict with their lances and their shields.
Hear, hear! Prolonged applause. Damn it all!
—Of course I'm a Britisher, Haines's voice said, and I feel as one. I don't want to see my country fall into the hands of German Jews either. That's our national problem, I'm afraid, just now.
Two men stood at the edge of the cliff, watching: a businessman, a boatman.
—She's making for Bullock harbor.
The boatman nodded toward the north of the bay with some disdain.
—There's five fathoms out there, he said. It'll be swept up that way when the tide comes in around one. It's nine days today.
The man who drowned. A sail veering about the blank bay, waiting for a swollen body to bob up, roll over to the sun a puffy face, salt-white. Here I am.

They followed the winding path down to the creek. Buck Mulligan stood on a stone, in shirtsleeves, his untied tie rippling over his shoulder. A young man clinging to a spur of rock near him moved slowly, frog-like, his green legs in the deep jelly of the water.
—Is the brother with you, Malachi?
—Down in Westmeath. With the Bannons.
—Still there? I got a card from Bannon. Says he found a sweet young thing down there. Photo girl he calls her.
—Snapshot, eh? Brief exposure.

Buck Mulligan sat down to unlace his boots. An elderly man surfaced near the spur of rock, his red face blowing. He scrambled up the stones, water glistening on his bald head and its garland of grey hair, water running over his chest and belly and spilling in jets from his black sagging swimsuit.
Buck Mulligan made way for him to scramble past and, glancing at Haines and Stephen, crossed himself mockingly with his thumbnail at brow and lips and chest.
—Seymour's back in town, the young man said, grasping his rock again. Dropped out of medical school and going in for the army.
—Oh, you're joking! Buck Mulligan said.
—Going to England next week to train. You know that red-haired Carlisle girl, Lily?
—Yes.
—Fooling around with him last night on the pier. The father is rolling in money.
—Is she pregnant?
—Better ask Seymour that.
—Seymour a bloody officer! Buck Mulligan said.
He nodded to himself as he pulled off his trousers and stood up, saying flatly:
—Redheaded women are wild in bed.
He broke off in alarm, feeling his side under his flapping shirt.
—My twelfth rib is gone, he cried. I'm the Superman. Toothless Kinch and I, the supermen.
He struggled out of his shirt and flung it behind him where his clothes lay.
—Are you going in here, Malachi?
—Yes. Make room in the bed.
The young man shoved himself backward through the water and reached the middle of the creek in two long clean strokes. Haines sat down on a stone, smoking.
—Are you not coming in? Buck Mulligan asked.
—Later on, Haines said. Not on my breakfast.
Stephen turned away.
—I'm going, Mulligan, he said.
—Give us that key, Kinch, Buck Mulligan said, to keep my shirt flat.
Stephen handed him the key. Buck Mulligan laid it across his heaped clothes.
—And twopence, he said, for a pint. Throw it there.
Stephen threw two pennies on the soft heap. Dressing, undressing. Buck Mulligan standing erect, with hands joined before him, said solemnly:
—He who steals from the poor lends to the Lord. Thus spoke Zarathustra.
His plump body plunged.
—We'll see you again, Haines said, turning as Stephen walked up the path and smiling at this wild Irishman.
Horn of a bull, hoof of a horse, smile of an Englishman.
—The Ship pub, Buck Mulligan cried. Half twelve.
—Good, Stephen said.
He walked along the upward-curving path.

Shining throng of confessors.
Let them surround you.
Choir of rejoicing virgins.
The priest's grey halo in a niche where he dressed discreetly. I will not sleep here tonight. Home also I cannot go.
A voice, sweet-toned and sustained, called to him from the sea. Turning the curve he waved his hand. It called again. A sleek brown head, a seal's, far out on the water, round.
Usurper.
